implementation_notes: Swift decorates through protocol conformance: a wrapper type - usually a struct - holds the wrapped value and conforms to the same protocol, forwarding each requirement explicitly, and value semantics make the wrapping copy explicit rather than hidden. The forwarding obligation is enforced by the protocol unless a protocol extension supplies a default implementation, which is also the trap: a decorator that omits a member silently inherits the default instead of delegating. Property wrappers (@propertyWrapper, SE-0258) are the compiler-supported decorator for a single property's access/storage, not for decorating objects, so they complement this form instead of replacing it; for protocols with associated types or mutating requirements the wrapper needs generics or a type-erasing AnyX box.
idiom_name: struct/class conforming to the component protocol, holding the wrapped value and forwarding its members
pitfalls: A protocol extension default implementation lets the decorator compile while never calling the wrapped value - the default runs instead of the inner implementation, and the decoration is silently a no-op.
Protocols with associated types, Self requirements or mutating methods cannot be forwarded through a plain struct; forwarding forces generics, class constraints or a type-erasing AnySender wrapper.
Wrapping a class in a struct still shares the same reference: dropping the wrapper does not undo mutations made through it, which is exactly the identity surprise the pattern is famous for.
